title: What Is Nodics?
readerIntent: Understand what Nodics is, why an organization would use it, how its main parts work together, and where to continue.
priorKnowledge: No Nodics or enterprise-framework knowledge is required.
summary: Nodics is a modular enterprise application platform and application factory for building secure, governed, API-driven, multi-tenant business products without forcing every project to recreate common enterprise capabilities.

sections.heading: What is What Is Nodics?
paragraphs: Nodics is an enterprise application platform and application factory for building modular, governed, API-driven business systems. It supplies reusable framework capabilities while allowing projects and partners to customize implementations through explicit layers.

Instead of beginning every application with unrelated infrastructure choices, a team starts from shared contracts for configuration, data, security, APIs, operations, extension, and testing, then composes the business capabilities the project actually needs.

sections.heading: The problem Nodics is designed to solve
paragraphs: Building an MVP is faster than ever, but scaling that MVP into a secure, governed, multi-team, multi-tenant product is still painfully hard. AI-assisted coding and rapid prototyping can create impressive demonstrations quickly. The problem starts when the demonstration becomes the real product and the team discovers that the codebase has no strong module boundaries, no layered architecture, no governance model, no safe customization path, weak security rules, limited test coverage, and no reliable way to evolve customer-specific behavior.

Many early applications were built only to prove an idea. As features accumulate, business logic is placed wherever a developer or AI tool first finds space; APIs, services, data access, and permissions become coupled; environment configuration is copied; customer behavior is added directly to core code; generated files are edited manually; tenant isolation and security are added late; and the application cannot be divided safely across runtime processes.

Nodics turns those recurring scaling problems into an explicit application model. It lets teams move with the speed of AI-assisted product development while keeping the architecture, governance, security, testing, operations, documentation, and extension discipline expected from an enterprise platform.

sections.heading: The MVP-to-scale bridge
paragraphs: Nodics lets a team start quickly without accepting a throwaway architecture. A feature created during an MVP still lands inside an owned capability, a supported layer, an authenticated API, a governed schema, an explicit configuration scope, and a verification contract.

The bridge is broader than moving from one process to several servers. It includes modular capability ownership instead of scattered code; layered customization instead of framework edits; tenant-aware behavior instead of hard-coded customers; preview, audit, and rollback for eligible runtime changes; built-in identity, permission, validation, and diagnostic patterns; generated contracts and tests; provider-neutral integrations; and documentation that keeps people and AI tools aligned.

A local monoServer can compose many modules for convenient development. Later, deployment can separate modules for scale, resilience, security, or team ownership without changing which capability owns the behavior. The result is a faster MVP path with a controlled route to production scale.

sections.heading: Nodics in plain language
paragraphs: Nodics is a foundation for building business applications. It gives a team working implementations and defined extension points for capabilities that enterprise applications repeatedly need: APIs, data models, users, permissions, configuration, scheduled work, events, workflows, imports, exports, caching, search, content, commerce, testing, and runtime operations.

Think of it as an application factory rather than a finished business application. A factory provides an organized production system, reusable equipment, safety rules, and quality checks. The product team still decides which business product to build. In the same way, Nodics provides the structure and reusable capabilities, while a customer or partner project supplies its own business rules, data, integrations, and user experiences.

A beginner does not need to memorize repository folders or internal module names. Start with the business outcome, identify the capability that owns it, understand its public contract, and use the documented configuration or extension path.

sections.heading: Why enterprise applications need a platform
paragraphs: A small application can begin with a few routes and database calls. As it grows, it normally needs authentication, authorization, tenant isolation, configuration, caching, search, background processing, data import, observability, audit evidence, deployment controls, and safe customer customization. If every project invents these concerns independently, delivery slows down and the application becomes difficult to secure or change.

Nodics provides common contracts for these concerns before they become emergencies. Product teams can spend more time on business differentiation, while architects and operators retain clear ownership, predictable runtime behavior, and evidence that important boundaries were tested.

sections.heading: The core design principle
paragraphs: Capabilities are sacred; implementations are negotiable.

This means the business promise of a capability should remain stable even when its implementation evolves. For example, an application depends on a cache capability rather than embedding Redis-specific code throughout business services. A project can choose an available provider or introduce a compliant provider without changing every caller.

The same rule applies to customer customization. A partner should first reuse an existing capability, then configure or extend it through a later layer, and create a new implementation only when the existing contract genuinely cannot satisfy the requirement. This avoids duplicate authority paths and keeps framework upgrades manageable.

sections.heading: How Nodics is organized
paragraphs: Every capability has an owner. Its configuration, schemas, services, APIs, tests, operational behavior, and implementation documentation belong with that owner. Other capabilities interact through the owner's public contracts instead of directly taking control of its data or runtime responsibility.

Nodics loads behavior through an ordered hierarchy. Reusable framework capabilities establish defaults. Business capability groups add domain behavior. A customer project and its environment, server, node, tenant, and runtime layers can refine those defaults. Later layers may customize an approved extension point, but they do not silently create a second framework.

This organization supports both people and tools. A developer can locate the correct place for a change, a reviewer can identify its authority, an operator can understand its runtime scope, and an AI tool can be told exactly which contracts it must preserve.

sections.heading: Backend, frontend, and business-logic boundaries
paragraphs: Nodics core is a backend and API platform. It owns business capabilities, data contracts, authentication and authorization, validation, workflows, integrations, runtime configuration, and operational behavior.

A frontend application is a separate process and repository. It renders pages and components, collects user input, and calls authorized backend APIs; it must not become a second home for business rules. Nodics Axis follows this model for employee BackOffice experiences. Customer storefronts and corporate sites follow the same separation.

This boundary lets several user experiences consume the same governed backend capability without copying its authority. It also allows frontend technology and presentation to evolve independently from backend deployment and data ownership.

sections.heading: From a local application to modular runtime
paragraphs: During early development, a team can run many active capabilities together in a consolidated local process. This reduces setup time and makes end-to-end development practical.

As scale, resilience, security, or team ownership requires separation, capabilities can run in different backend processes. Environment configuration determines which modules are local, which are remote, and how remote APIs are reached. The unit of ownership remains the module capability; a server is only a runtime grouping.
This makes the MVP-to-scale path evolutionary. The team does not need to rewrite the application merely because it moves from one local process to a distributed topology.

sections.heading: Security and governance are built into the model
paragraphs: Nodics treats security as a system contract. Human username-and-password authentication remains separate from module-to-module and scheduled-process access. Authorization is evaluated by the capability that owns the requested operation, and tenant context must not become a client-controlled shortcut around isolation.

Sensitive runtime changes can use preview, request, approval, activation, audit, diagnostics, and rollback behavior. Import, publishing, workflow, scheduled execution, and administration operations are expected to expose both positive and negative evidence.

The framework supplies mechanisms, but a deployed solution still has shared responsibilities. Project teams must configure credentials safely, grant least privilege, protect infrastructure, monitor the application, test their extensions, and keep supported versions current.

sections.heading: A concrete example
paragraphs: Suppose a retailer needs an employee application for managing two websites: Apparel and Electronics. Both websites belong to one enterprise and tenant but use different content catalogs, storefront settings, stock availability, and prices.

The content capability owns pages and components. Storefront owns hostname and site context. Stock owns availability. Pricing owns price selection. Profile owns employees and permissions. Workflow and publishing coordinate reviewed changes from staged systems to online systems. Axis renders the employee interface and calls each owning backend capability directly after authorization.

A partner can customize the retailer's rules in its project modules and configuration. It does not copy these capabilities into the frontend or modify reusable Nodics source for one customer. The result is a solution tailored to the retailer while the platform contracts remain reusable.

sections.heading: What Nodics is not
items: It is not a frontend design system or a place to embed browser presentation code.
It is not a single finished product that removes the need for project-specific business analysis.
It is not permission to bypass owning-module APIs and access another capability's database directly.
It is not a collection of interchangeable folders where code can be placed wherever it first works.
It does not make production operations automatic; deployment architecture, capacity, monitoring, credentials, recovery, and compliance still require governed decisions.

sections.heading: Common Commands
paragraphs: Use the repository runtime contract before installing dependencies. The preferred release line is Node.js 24 with npm 11. Node.js 22 remains in the supported validation matrix, and Node.js 26 is for forward validation as it moves toward LTS. Do not use Node.js 25 as a release target.
Install dependencies:

```bash
npm ci
```
Use `npm install` only when intentionally changing dependencies, and commit `package.json` and `package-lock.json` together.
Build generated artifacts and documentation outputs:

```bash
npm run build
```
Start Nodics:

```bash
npm run start
```
Start with debugger support:

```bash
npm run start:debug
```
Run the main test gate:

```bash
npm run test:basic
```
Run the full test gate:

```bash
npm run test:full
```
Print the clean-checkout release gate:

```bash
npm run release:check
```
Execute it when preparing a release candidate:

```bash
npm run release:check -- --execute --full
```

sections.heading: Complete guide: What Nodics Is
paragraphs: Nodics is an enterprise application factory for building modular, governed, API-driven business platforms.

It is more than a web framework and more than a collection of utilities. Nodics gives an application a complete operating structure: modules, APIs, schemas, services, permissions, tenants, runtime configuration, scheduled jobs, events, imports, exports, search indexing, catalog and content capabilities, tests, generated artifacts, deployment topology, and documentation.
![Nodics Architecture](../assets/images/nodics-architecture.jpg)

sections.heading: Beginner Summary
paragraphs: Nodics helps you build serious applications without starting from a blank folder. It gives you ready places for common enterprise needs: APIs, users, permissions, data models, import/export, cache, search, jobs, events, workflow, tests, configuration, deployment topology, and documentation.
The most important beginner idea is:

```text
Every feature must have an owner and a correct layer.
```
For example:

| If you need | You usually work in |
| --- | --- |
| A new API | router, controller, facade, service |
| A new data model | schema and generated tests |
| A business rule | service or facade |
| A database provider | database provider module |
| A cache rule | cache configuration/service |
| A scheduled task | cronjob definition and service |
| A tenant-specific difference | tenant/runtime configuration or later project module |
| A customer-specific behavior | customer/project module |
This structure is useful for humans and AI tools because it reduces guessing. Instead of putting code anywhere, the framework tells you where the code should live and how to verify it.

Instead of putting all code in one application folder, Nodics organizes behavior into active capabilities. A capability can provide data models, APIs, services, scheduled jobs, events, import/export behavior, permissions, tests, and documentation. A project can then extend or replace behavior through later-loaded project modules without editing framework files.

Nodics is also built for AI-assisted development. Developers can use CLI-based AI tools, IDE assistants, or conversational coding tools to describe what they want to build. Nodics gives those tools a governed structure to follow so generated or assisted code lands in the right place and respects the same rules as human-written code.

sections.heading: What Problem Nodics Solves
paragraphs: Many enterprise applications start simple and then become hard to maintain:
Nodics solves this by giving every capability a clear place to live, a clear way to be extended, and a clear way to be verified.

That is the main reason Nodics is valuable for AI-assisted MVP development. A team can move quickly with command-line AI tools, IDE assistants, or conversational coding tools, but the generated work still lands inside a governed platform model instead of becoming scattered prototype code that is painful to scale later.
The core rule is:

```text
Capabilities are stable. Implementations can change.
```

For example, Nodics can provide a default database capability. A project can add a new database provider or change data access behavior through the module hierarchy, but it does not edit the original framework source just to serve one customer.
This makes Nodics especially strong for customer-specific enterprise work. The framework provides stable capabilities, while projects negotiate the implementation through approved extension layers.

sections.heading: Technology Stack
paragraphs: Nodics uses Node.js and JavaScript as the runtime foundation for modular API development. It builds on common enterprise application concerns such as Express-style request handling, schema-driven data behavior, database providers, cache providers, search providers, messaging providers, scheduled execution, import/export processing, generated artifacts, and automated tests.
![Nodics Technology Stack](../assets/images/technology-stack.jpg)

The stack is intentionally layered. Application developers should depend on Nodics capability contracts such as schemas, services, routers, pipelines, events, cache, search, import/export, and configuration. Provider-specific behavior belongs behind provider modules so a project can change MongoDB, Cassandra, Redis, search, messaging, file, or integration behavior without rewriting business capabilities.

sections.heading: Main Ideas
paragraphs: Nodics is based on a few simple ideas.
**Modules own capabilities.** A module owns the behavior, configuration, schemas, tests, and documentation for the feature it provides.

**Projects extend through layers.** A customer project adds or overrides behavior through project modules, environment modules, server modules, node modules, tenant configuration, runtime configuration, or data. It does not modify released framework code unless the work is explicitly framework maintenance.
**Configuration is layered.** Defaults come from the framework. Projects, environments, servers, nodes, tenants, and runtime configuration can refine behavior later in the hierarchy.

**Generated files come from source definitions.** Regenerate generated APIs, schemas, tests, OpenAPI output, and LLM context from the owning source. Do not hand-maintain generated output as the source of truth.
**Security is part of the contract.** Authentication, authorization, access control, validation, audit, rollback, diagnostics, and tests are not optional extras.
